title: Pauri 8, sound: suniai
tomorrow: Pauri 8, meaning: the power of listening

segments.voice: Yesterday, nadar, and the turn of pauri seven: famous for ages, and still, without the glance, no one asks after you. Your line was fame is not it. Did one good thing go unmentioned? Day one hundred seventy-seven.

Back at the start of this camp, on Japji Sahib, we said Japji would give four whole pauris to one word. Today is the day that word arrives. It's a soft word, almost a sigh, and once you've heard it you'll hear it all through this part of Japji, because for four pauris straight it starts nearly every line. If you've ever sat in a gurdwara at dawn while Japji is recited, this is the stretch where the word rolls around and around the room like a wave coming in.
screen: `FOUR PAURIS FOR ONE WORD.` → `A SOFT WORD, ALMOST A SIGH.` → `A WAVE COMING IN.`

segments.voice: The word is suniai. Let's sound it: SUN-i-ai. The first syllable is like soon, but short, closer to the u in put. Then a light i. Then ai, a little like the start of air. Sun-i-ai. The n in the middle, in Gurmukhi, is the one made with the tongue curled back, the same n you heard at the end of taan in pauri three. Suniai comes from sunnaa, to hear, to listen, and the ending means something like by, or through. So: by listening. Through hearing. The opening line of pauri eight: suniai sidh peer sur naath. Sidh: siddhas, yogis said to have gained great powers. Peer: pirs, the Sufi masters, the spiritual guides of Muslim Punjab. Sur: the gods. Naath: the naths, masters of a yogic order; the stories of Guru Nanak's travels have him meeting and talking with them. So in one breath the line names holy people of many kinds from Guru Nanak's world, and says they came to be what they are by listening. Now listen to the rhythm of the whole stretch. Pauri eight: suniai, suniai, suniai, suniai. Pauri nine, the same. Pauri ten, the same. Pauri eleven, the same. Line after line opening on the same soft word. Japji keeps that drumbeat going for four whole pauris. And every one of these four pauris ends on the same two lines, a refrain about devotees being always in bloom. We'll open all of that tomorrow. For today, one word is enough. Suniai. By listening.
screen: `SUNIAI — BY LISTENING.` · `SIDH, PEER, SUR, NAATH.` · `HOLY PEOPLE OF MANY KINDS.` · `FOUR PAURIS, ONE DRUMBEAT.` · then, large: `SUNIAI.`

segments.voice: Say the word slowly, five times, with a breath between each one. Suniai. Breathe. Suniai. Breathe. Suniai. Breathe. Suniai. Breathe. Suniai. Now stop speaking, and do what the word says. Listen. The room, the street, your own breath, the small hum of whatever machine is nearby. Don't name anything. Just receive it. If you pray, you can let Waheguru be the last sound before the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Suniai. By listening. The soft word that opens nearly every line of Japji's pauris eight to eleven.
Your line: suniai, listening. Today, in one conversation, let the other person finish completely before you start. Day one hundred seventy-seven.

original.note: Gurmukhi: suniai, by listening. the ਣ is a retroflex n.

trapdoor: what it means: by listening, through hearing: the word that opens nearly every line of pauris eight to eleven.
what a scholar hears: suniai is a form of sunnaa, to hear; the stretch that follows (mannai) turns from hearing to trusting what is heard.

notes: Glosses of sidh, peer, sur, naath: confirm (sur as gods/devas; naath as Nath yogis).
Guru Nanak meeting Nath yogis on his travels (Sidh Gosht tradition): confirm phrasing.
